title: What is the Smallest Unit of Memory?
content_html:
What is the Smallest Unit of Memory?

There is no single indivisible “atom” of memory. Granularity depends on the level of description — from molecular switches to synapses to engram ensembles to cognitive chunks to information-theoretic bits.

Molecular Switches

  • CaMKII/PP1 bistable switching; CaMKII–NMDAR complexes proposed for late-LTP maintenance.
  • CPEB prion-like state stabilizes local protein synthesis for durable traces.

Candidate “microstates” that can persist and modulate synapses.

Plastic Synapses

  • LTP/LTD modifies efficacy via receptor trafficking and spine remodeling.
  • Multi-state/metaplastic models expand capacity and retention.

Often treated as the elementary neural unit of storage.

Engram Cells

  • Memories are distributed ensembles whose reactivation retrieves content.
  • Tag-and-manipulate experiments identify and causally test engrams.

A single neuron rarely suffices; it’s the pattern that matters.

Chunks & Features

  • Immediate memory limited; organization via chunking.
  • Episodes have hierarchical granularity (moments → scenes → events).

Units are task and schema-dependent, not fixed.

Bits under Noise

  • Discriminations (bits) realized in noisy, redundant circuits.
  • Trade-offs: capacity vs. longevity vs. interference.

Neural “bits” are probabilistic, distributed, and error-tolerant.

If you must name a smallest unit: at the biophysical scale, propose a molecular switch state (e.g., CaMKII or CPEB); at the neural scale, a change in a synapse; at the psychological scale, a chunk/feature; but real memories are distributed reconstructions across these layers.
